clue.text: Prone to quarrel? Not in this sort of fight

definitions.text: Prone to quarrel? Not in this sort of fight

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who is quick to pick a fight

blocks.clueFragment: Not in this sort of fight
blocks.note: setter's reading: prone means lying flat, and in this kind of fight nobody lies down

explanation.surface: Someone touchy about arguments is told this kind of brawl is not for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prone' looks like 'inclined to', but it is the literal sense, lying face down. A STAND-UP fight is one where the fighters stay on their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-up fight is a straightforward toe-to-toe brawl, fought upright rather than on the ground.

clue.text: Withdraw for Yuletide up in Bishop's place

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top
one thing in a place means it sits inside the other

blocks.note: Yuletide falls in December, abbreviated Dec
a bishop's see is the area under his authority

explanation.surface: A cleric goes into retreat over Christmas in the bishop's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: SEE is a bishop's diocese or seat, a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To secede is to withdraw formally from a union or organisation, as states do from a federation.

clue.text: One in company overcome by a knave cut off in Corsica

definitions.note: the answer is a town in Corsica, not the island itself

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece overcome by another sits below it, so the other comes first
cut off means the word loses its last letter
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
the knave in a pack of cards is also called the jack
I is the Roman numeral one
Co. is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: Someone in a group is beaten by a scoundrel who is stranded on a Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: Ajaccio is the capital of Corsica and Napoleon's birthplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Ajaccio is the main town and port on the west coast of Corsica, so it is a place found on the island.

clue.text: In Ireland a grey-brown nag turns up? No, in France

definitions.note: names the town only by where it is

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown colour
taken as written
non is French for no

explanation.surface: An Irish horse of dull colour arrives, or perhaps it is a French one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No, in France' looks like the setter changing its mind about the location; it is French for no. Dungannon is a town in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Dungannon is a market town in County Tyrone, so it is a place to be found in Ireland.

clue.text: Certain light admissions may lead to these developments

definitions.text: Certain light admissions may lead to these developments

blocks.note: surface reading: casual confessions, admissions made lightly
setter's reading: letting light into a camera, an exposure, leads to film that is then developed

explanation.surface: A few offhand confessions can set events moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light admissions' means letting light in, and 'developments' is the darkroom sense of developing film.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographs are produced by exposing film to light and then developing it chemically into prints.

clue.text: Such walls as Lovelace's imagination surmounted

definitions.text: Such walls as Lovelace's imagination surmounted

blocks.note: surface reading: some kind of barrier a poet's mind could rise above
setter's reading: Lovelace wrote 'Stone walls do not a prison make', so the walls were of stone, built by masons

explanation.surface: A poet in prison lets his imagination soar over the walls holding him.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Lovelace's poem To Althea, from Prison begins 'Stone walls do not a prison make'. Stone walls are the work of masons. This is a weak fit and the answer is not certain.
explanation.definitionFit: Masonic is used loosely here to mean of masons' work, that is built of stone, like the prison walls in the poem.

clue.text: Wallowing hippos? What larks!

blocks.note: setter's reading: what hippos wallow in
surface reading: an exclamation of fun; but put the answer before larks and you get boys who scavenge on riverbanks

explanation.surface: Someone delights in the sight of hippopotamuses rolling about.
explanation.walkthrough: Flanders and Swann's Hippopotamus Song has the chorus 'Mud, mud, glorious mud'. Mudlarks were children who scavenged in Thames mud, and 'What larks' is Joe Gargery's catchphrase in Great Expectations.
explanation.definitionFit: Mud is the wet soft earth that hippopotamuses wallow in to keep cool.

clue.text: Leafy drink

definitions.note: adjective, while the answer is a noun: a leafy plant

blocks.note: first meaning: a bush, a woody leafy plant
second meaning: an old drink of rum or brandy with fruit juice and sugar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leafy drink' sounds like a herbal tea; the two words are separate. Shrub as a drink is an old cordial of spirits and fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrub is a small woody plant covered in leaves, and also an old-fashioned fruit-and-spirit cordial.

clue.text: Pen has a tongue-wag at the club

blocks.note: a nib is the writing point of a pen, standing for the whole
a lick is a stroke of the tongue

explanation.surface: A writer gossips with the members at his club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue-wag' suggests chatter at a gentlemen's club; it is a lick, and the club is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A niblick is an old Scottish name for a lofted iron golf club, roughly today's nine iron.

clue.text: Benjamin Faithful

definitions.note: a first name, standing for the writer who bore it

blocks.note: first meaning: Benjamin ..., the Swiss-born French writer and politician, author of Adolphe
second meaning: loyal and unchanging

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like a person's full name; the surname to complete Benjamin is the answer, and it also means loyal.
explanation.definitionFit: Constant means steadfast and loyal, as in a constant companion, and Benjamin Constant was a noted French liberal writer.

clue.text: Burn black north forest of Leicestershire

blocks.note: to char is to burn something until it turns black
N is the standard abbreviation for north
a wood is a small forest

explanation.surface: Fire blackens a forest in the north of an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'forest' does double duty, supplying the last piece and also belonging to the definition. Charnwood Forest is upland in north-west Leicestershire, an English county in the Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Charnwood Forest is a named area of hilly woodland and heath in the county of Leicestershire, England.

clue.text: Dressin' for the ceremony — with red waistcoat

definitions.note: robin' is robing with its last letter dropped, as the apostrophe in dressin' signals
describes the bird rather than naming it

blocks.note: first meaning: ...', putting on robes for a ceremony, dropping the final g in the same way as dressin'
second meaning: the ... redbreast, a small bird with a red chest

explanation.surface: Someone puts on formal dress for an occasion, complete with a scarlet waistcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g of 'Dressin'' tells you the answer also drops one: robin' for robing.
explanation.definitionFit: Robing is putting on ceremonial robes, and the robin is the familiar bird whose red breast looks like a waistcoat.

clue.text: Bill the Bounder back in the city

indicators.note: going back means the joined pieces are read from right to left

blocks.note: AC, short for account, is a bill
a bounder is an old word for a cad, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A rogue called Bill has come back to town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill the Bounder' reads like a nickname; it is two separate pieces. Dacca is the older spelling of Dhaka, capital of Bangladesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Dacca, now usually spelt Dhaka, is the capital and largest urban centre of Bangladesh.

clue.text: Duma's fall guy of 1905

blocks.note: surface reading: a scapegoat who took the blame for the Russian parliament's failings
setter's reading: fall is autumn, so a man named after an autumn month, a member of the party founded after the 1905 manifesto

explanation.surface: Someone took the blame for the Russian parliament's troubles in 1905.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall guy' wants to mean scapegoat; read it as an autumn man. The Octobrists were a Russian party formed to support the Tsar's October Manifesto of 1905, which created the Duma.
explanation.definitionFit: An Octobrist was a member of the moderate Russian party that sat in the Duma, the parliament set up after 1905.

clue.text: He usually has something in the pipe-line

definitions.text: He usually has something in the pipe-line

blocks.note: surface reading: a man who always has a plan on the way
setter's reading: a shopkeeper whose line of trade is filling pipes

explanation.surface: A busy man always has a new project coming along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipe-line' wants to mean in preparation; read it as a line of goods for pipes.
explanation.definitionFit: A tobacconist is a shopkeeper selling tobacco, cigars and smoking equipment, so pipe tobacco is his stock.

clue.text: Rustic type of family knocker

blocks.note: rustic means belonging to the country
a bump is a knock
your kin are your family

explanation.surface: A yokel is the sort of person who goes hammering on relatives' doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rustic' serves both the definition and the first piece, and 'family knocker' is read in reverse order, knock then family. The parse is loose but the phrase is certain.
explanation.definitionFit: A country bumpkin is an unsophisticated person from the countryside, the stock rural yokel.

clue.text: Where .Kitty awaits Mickey

blocks.note: surface reading: a girl's name, perhaps waiting for a boyfriend
setter's reading: a cat watching for a mouse at the place it will come out

explanation.surface: A girl waits for her date at their meeting place.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitty is a cat and Mickey a mouse, after Mickey Mouse. The stray dot before Kitty is a printing mark. Mousehole is also a Cornish fishing village.
explanation.definitionFit: A mousehole is the small opening in a wall or skirting board where a mouse lives, and where a cat lies in wait.

clue.text: All may go swimmingly in their walk of life

definitions.text: All may go swimmingly in their walk of life

blocks.note: surface reading: everything goes smoothly for some group of people
setter's reading: creatures whose way of life is both swimming and walking, in water and on land

explanation.surface: For people in a certain profession, everything goes smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmingly' and 'walk of life' are idioms for success and career; taken literally, they are the two halves of a frog's life.
explanation.definitionFit: Amphibia is the class of animals such as frogs and newts that live both in water and on land.

clue.text: Emotive, these works of art? Not still

definitions.text: Emotive, these works of art? Not still

blocks.note: surface reading: paintings that stir the feelings
setter's reading: images that are not stills but are in motion, as at the cinema

explanation.surface: Paintings so stirring they could hardly be called still lifes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emotive' points to moving in the sense of touching, and 'Not still' to moving in the sense of in motion; both apply to films.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving pictures is the old name for films, pictures that move rather than stand still like a photograph.

clue.text: Madly over-gay, he could finish in the drink

definitions.text: he could finish in the drink

indicators.note: something done madly is wild and disordered, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: A reckless reveller might end up falling into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is slang for the sea, where a voyage may end.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyager travels by sea, so a journey that goes wrong may see him end up in the water.

clue.text: Fanny's old mother turns up blue

definitions.note: possessive: Fanny Burney's, naming her novel by its author

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word that follows is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Eve, the first woman, is the oldest mother of all in Genesis
anil is the indigo plant and its blue dye

explanation.surface: Fanny's elderly mother arrives looking miserable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like a mood; it is the dye anil. Fanny Burney wrote the novel Evelina (1778), so Fanny is the author, not someone's name in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Evelina is the first and most famous novel by Fanny Burney, so it is Fanny's book.

clue.text: May she in fancy be least among goddesses?

definitions.note: plural, while the answer is one goddess among them

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the following words, running across them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A modest question whether some goddess might be imagined as the humblest of them all.
explanation.walkthrough: Cybele is the Phrygian mother goddess, worshipped in Rome as the Great Mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Cybele was an Anatolian mother goddess of nature, one of the deities of the Greek and Roman world.

clue.text: Country dance, quick time, brings out the rabbits

definitions.note: the answer is an exclamation; the definition describes what it accompanies

blocks.note: a hey, also spelt hay, is an old English country dance
presto is the musical direction for a very quick tempo

explanation.surface: A lively rural jig at a fast tempo sends the rabbits scattering from their burrows.
explanation.walkthrough: The rabbits are not in a field but in a conjuror's hat: hey presto is what the magician says as one appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Hey presto is the stage magician's exclamation at the moment of a trick, such as producing a rabbit from a hat.

clue.text: Wild Irish sage

indicators.note: wild means untamed and disorderly, so the letters run loose

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An untamed Irishman turns out to be a wise man.
explanation.definitionFit: A rishi is a Hindu holy man or seer, a wise teacher in the Vedic tradition.

clue.text: Verses for example in city or rural fane's precincts

indicators.note: one thing in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: e.g. is the abbreviation of for example
Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A poem set in town or in the grounds of a country church.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is an allusion: a fane is a temple, so a rural fane's precincts is a country churchyard, recalling Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a poem of lament, a set of mournful verses, and Gray's is the most famous in English.

clue.text: Let us down as Christian was let down? Can't be true

blocks.clueFragment: down as Christian was let down
blocks.note: in The Pilgrim's Progress, Christian falls into the Slough of Despond, a bog, so to let someone down that way is to bog them
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pilgrim's mishap is used to warn that some story is false.
explanation.walkthrough: Christian is the hero of Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, who sinks into the Slough of Despond; 'let us down' is read as bog us.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bogus is fake or counterfeit, so it cannot be genuine; the definition is a phrase meaning untrue.

clue.text: Anti-torpedo device before the bustle

definitions.note: describes the garment by its place in fashion history

blocks.note: first meaning: naval slang for the steel net hung round a warship to stop torpedoes
second meaning: the hooped petticoat that was in fashion before the bustle replaced it

explanation.surface: A naval defence is fitted in the hurry before the action starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bustle' looks like activity; it is the padded frame worn under a skirt at the back, which followed the hooped skirt in the 1870s.
explanation.definitionFit: A crinoline was a stiff hooped petticoat of the mid-Victorian era, and the hanging torpedo net on warships was nicknamed after it.

clue.text: Creature more welcome on the lap than on the back

definitions.text: Creature more welcome on the lap than on the back

blocks.note: setter's reading: a pet curled up on someone's knees
setter's second reading: the whip with nine tails once used for floggings

explanation.surface: Some animal is happier sitting on your knee than riding on your shoulders.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat o' nine tails was a many-thonged whip used to flog sailors and prisoners on the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat is a common pet that sits on laps, and the same word names the flogging whip.

clue.text: Thermal transport?

blocks.note: surface reading: to do with heat, perhaps a warm vehicle
setter's reading: a thermal is a rising current of warm air that carries a glider up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thermal' looks like an adjective about heat; as a noun it is the column of rising air that gliders and birds ride.
explanation.definitionFit: An airlift is the carrying of goods or people by aircraft, and a thermal literally lifts things on air.

clue.text: Neat gee, frisky, young

indicators.note: frisky means skittish and lively, so the letters jump about out of order

blocks.note: neat is old for cattle and gee is a horse; the letters are taken as written

explanation.surface: A tidy horse turns playful, as young animals do.
explanation.definitionFit: Teenage describes someone in their teens, an adolescent, so in the sense of youthful it matches young.
